Let’s talk about something that’s both tough and transformative: Forgiveness, Grief, and Letting Go.
There’s this common myth out there—that healing means you have to forgive and forget, or somehow repair the relationship no matter what. But if you’re the daughter of a narcissistic mother, you know it’s rarely that simple.
Forgiveness, if you ever reach it, isn’t about brushing aside the pain or pretending the past didn’t happen. Instead, it’s about releasing the grip that anger and resentment have on you.
And grief? It’s a necessary part of the journey. It’s that deep sorrow for all the things you lost—a childhood that could have been, a mother who couldn’t give what you needed. Think about those moments when you see friends and their moms sharing laughter and warmth. There’s an ache, right? You might mourn the mother you wished for, or the parts of yourself that never got to shine.
Letting go doesn’t always mean cutting off all contact. For some, that’s the healthiest choice, but for others, it’s about accepting you might never get the apology or understanding you’ve hoped for. It’s about making peace with your past, so it doesn’t have the power to shape your present anymore.
Most of us don’t even realize how much energy we spend wishing things were different. When you finally let go of that hope, you make space for something new—self-acceptance, new connections, maybe even joy you didn’t expect.
Remember, this process isn’t a straight line. Grief and anger can pop up when you least expect them. But each time they do, the sting fades a little more, and suddenly, the future starts to feel just a bit more open.
